clue.text: Female caught by god early in the breeding season — that's what we hear

definitions.text: early in the breeding season — that's what we hear

parts.note: Dawn is a woman's name
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
Horus is the falcon-headed Egyptian sky god

explanation.surface: A woman is seized by a deity at mating time, and that is the noise people hear.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase: in spring, the breeding season, birds sing together at first light.
explanation.definitionFit: Birdsong at first light is loudest in spring, when birds sing to attract mates and defend territory.

clue.text: Notice power being grabbed by churchman, showing no emotion

indicators.note: being grabbed by means these pieces are held inside the next word

parts.note: a dean is a senior clergyman
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: A cleric seizes control, keeping a straight face.
explanation.definitionFit: A blank, expressionless face, especially when joking, is described this way.

clue.text: Where you'll get channel hopping, of course

definitions.text: Where you'll get channel hopping, of course

parts.words: Where you'll get channel hopping, of course
parts.note: 'channel hopping' read as horses leaping a ditch of water, on a steeplechase course

explanation.surface: Of course, this is where you will flick between TV stations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'channel hopping' looks like flicking TV channels and 'of course' like 'naturally', but the course is a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: On a steeplechase course this obstacle is a fence with a ditch of water that horses must clear.

clue.text: Getting the bird, casually drew nil-nil after a part of 1 ac

indicators.note: after means the doodling and nil-nil pieces follow the single letter

parts.note: a cock is a male bird
to doodle is to draw idly
two O's, each a zero

explanation.surface: Booed off, a team played a goalless draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting the bird' looks like being booed, but simply supplies COCK. '1 ac' is the first across answer: the cockerel's crow is part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The cockerel's crow at first light belongs to the chorus of birdsong at that hour.

clue.text: Leg hit in front of garage?

definitions.meaning: in cricket, a drive to the leg (on) side of the field
read as '...', parked on the driveway before a garage

explanation.surface: A leg was struck outside the garage.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, 'leg' and 'on' both name the side of the field behind the batsman's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A batting stroke driven to the leg side, and a car standing on the driveway.

clue.text: Improve upon grub at deli with halves all round

indicators.note: each word in turn gives up only its front half, so halves are taken all round

explanation.surface: Make food at a delicatessen better.
explanation.walkthrough: Halves: UP from upon, GR from grub, A from at, DE from deli.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise to a higher standard or grade is to make better.

clue.text: Captives returned in exchange

indicators.note: returned means the word for the captives is read back to front

parts.note: POWs are prisoners of war

explanation.surface: Prisoners are sent home as part of a swap deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' looks like the prisoners going home, but it signals the word turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A swop, an older spelling of swap, is a trade of one thing for another.

clue.text: Sources acquired by boring author

definitions.meaning: springs of water reached by drilling into the ground
H G ..., writer of The War of the Worlds

explanation.surface: A dull writer obtains his material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like tedious, but it means drilling.
explanation.definitionFit: Holes drilled for water or oil are sources, and the surname of the science-fiction novelist H G Wells.

clue.text: Queen, in fall, put up monument

indicators.note: put up in a down answer means the letters are written upwards, back to front
in means the queen goes inside the word for fall

parts.note: a dip is a fall, a drop
Mary is the name of several queens

explanation.surface: A queen erected a memorial during autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall' looks like autumn but means a dip; 'in' puts the queen inside it and 'put up' turns the whole thing upwards in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The great tombs of the pharaohs at Giza are the most famous monuments of this shape.

clue.text: Characters as heard on radio in play

definitions.meaning: in the radio alphabet the letters R and J are said as these two names
Shakespeare's tragedy of two young lovers

explanation.surface: The cast of a radio drama are in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people in a drama, but here it means letters as spoken in the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy of star-crossed lovers, and the radio code words for R and J.

clue.text: Classical form of shape that's under roof

definitions.meaning: ... is the classical Greek dialect of Athens, and an ... order or base is a classical style in architecture
the room or space at the very top of a house, under the roof

explanation.surface: An architect describes the classical outline of a loft.
explanation.definitionFit: The top-floor loft space is called by this name, which also denotes the elegant classical style of ancient Athens.

clue.text: Neckwear in the cloth one requires

definitions.meaning: a stiff white collar worn round the neck
'the cloth' is the clergy, so a member of it needs this clerical collar

explanation.surface: A tailor says that a garment for the neck is needed in fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the cloth' looks like fabric, but it means the clergy, as in 'a man of the cloth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy wear a white band-style collar as a badge of their office.

clue.text: Almost appreciate being maltreated by each head?

indicators.note: something maltreated is knocked about, so these letters are rearranged
almost means the word appreciate loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone nearly values being badly treated by every boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims APPRECIATE to APPRECIAT, which 'being maltreated' rearranges. The question mark flags 'head' as a person counted, not a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means for each person, literally by heads, as in income calculated for every member of a population.

clue.text: Which course would 'be purgative were condiments added?

definitions.text: Which course would 'be purgative were condiments added?

parts.words: Which course would 'be purgative were condiments added?
parts.note: the course is a racecourse; adding condiments (salts) to its name gives a well-known laxative

explanation.surface: A diner wonders which dish would act as a laxative with seasoning added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' looks like a dish at a meal, but it is a racecourse in Surrey, home of the Derby. Its name plus 'salts' names a laxative mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: This Surrey town has a famous racecourse, and the salts named after its springs are a traditional purgative.

clue.text: Special cell in northern Europe quietly replaced by noon

indicators.note: replaced by means one letter gives way to another in what came before

parts.note: taken as written
P stands for piano, quietly in music

explanation.surface: A special prison cell in the far north of Europe is quietly swapped at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: In N EUROPE, the P (quietly) is swapped for N (noon).
explanation.definitionFit: A nerve cell, specialised to carry electrical signals, is called this in British spelling.

clue.text: Went by pedaloes when stormy, none the less

indicators.note: a stormy sea tosses things about, so these letters are rearranged
the less means the letter that follows is taken away from the boat word

parts.note: O looks like nought, nothing

explanation.surface: People went past in pedal boats during a storm all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'none the less' looks like 'nevertheless', but splits as O (none) taken away by 'the less' from PEDALOES; 'when stormy' rearranges PEDALES.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that has passed or gone by is said to have run its course.

clue.text: Spree almost accepted by hard-up Scrooge

indicators.note: accepted by means the shortened spree goes inside the word for broke

parts.note: skint is British slang for having no money

indicators.note: almost means the word for a spree loses its final letter

parts.note: a fling is a short spell of fun

explanation.surface: A miser takes on a near-binge while broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last letter of the spree word, and 'accepted by' puts the rest inside the British slang for broke.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge of Dickens is the archetypal miser, mean with money.

clue.text: Pup with waggly tail he'd confused and excited

indicators.note: confused letters are mixed up, so these are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a tail is the hind end, so the last letter of waggly

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A puppy with a wagging tail is said to be muddled and thrilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail' gives the Y ending 'waggly'; PUP, Y and HED are rearranged by 'confused'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone worked up into a state of agitation or enthusiasm is overstimulated, hyper.

clue.text: Expert stating the flaming obvious?

definitions.meaning: read as '...', saying that something on fire is hot

explanation.surface: A specialist says what everybody already knows.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as HOT'S HOT, a statement as obvious as saying fire is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A highly skilled, successful person is a crack performer, an ace.

clue.text: Bit on Tyneside runs North to South, perhaps

parts.note: a part is a bit, a portion
Tyneside, round Newcastle, is in the north-east of England, NE
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A piece of Tyneside stretches from top to bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the players sit as compass points, so North and South play together.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, North plays as the ally of South, sitting opposite at the table.

clue.text: Morse, say, taking in drug as sedative

parts.note: Morse is an example of a code
taken as written
E is slang for ecstasy

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse is taking a drug to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Morse' suggests the TV detective, but here it is the dot-and-dash signalling system.
explanation.definitionFit: This opiate painkiller also calms and induces drowsiness, so it serves as a sedative.

clue.text: Play's ready to begin? Gets stitches

definitions.meaning: read as '...', the actors are on stage
starts knitting by putting the first loops on the needle

explanation.surface: A show is about to start, and someone needs stitches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stitches' suggests sewing up a wound, but it is knitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitter starting work loops the first stitches on to the needle, and a stage company being in place.

clue.text: Closely examine projectile with detective

parts.note: a private eye is a detective
a ball is something thrown

explanation.surface: Study a missile alongside an investigator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' puts the two pieces together; the detective comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare at something hard, scrutinising it at close range.

clue.text: Either part of perfect present, perhaps

definitions.text: Either part of perfect present, perhaps

parts.words: Either part of perfect present, perhaps
parts.note: 'perfect' and 'present' read as grammar terms: each word names a form of a verb marking time

explanation.surface: A shopper thinks of half of an ideal gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perfect present' looks like an ideal gift, but each word is a grammatical term for a verb form.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect and present are both forms of a verb showing when an action happens.

clue.text: Plane crashed into mountainous region

indicators.note: a crashed plane is wrecked, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An aircraft came down in the mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: This Himalayan country contains Everest and most of the world's highest peaks.

clue.text: Result of this in cabinet, can it be?

definitions.text: Result of this in cabinet, can it be?

parts.words: Result of this in cabinet, can it be?
parts.note: the government cabinet is rearranged, and 'can it be' is itself a mix of letters from 'in cabinet'

explanation.surface: A minister asks whether some outcome in the cabinet is possible.
explanation.walkthrough: A prime minister changes ministers' jobs in a cabinet shake-up; the letters of 'cabinet' rearranged appear in 'can it be'.
explanation.definitionFit: A prime minister swapping round the posts of ministers is the standard name for a shake-up of government.

clue.text: They're often replaced in up-to date dives

parts.note: hip means fashionable, up-to-date
joints and dives are both slang for seedy bars

explanation.surface: Modern sleazy bars often get refitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dives' looks like a verb, but it is a noun for low-grade bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Worn ball-and-socket articulations at the pelvis are commonly swapped for artificial ones by surgeons.

clue.text: Informal 'dealings on island, a Mediterranean one

indicators.note: in an across answer, on means the dealings piece is placed after the island letter

parts.note: biz is informal for business, dealings

explanation.surface: Casual business on an island in the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' in the definition points back to 'island', so the Mediterranean island is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This Balearic isle off Spain lies in the Mediterranean Sea.

clue.text: Legendary Swiss count

definitions.meaning: William ..., the folk hero who shot an apple off his son's head

explanation.surface: A Swiss nobleman of legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'count' looks like a nobleman, but it is the old verb meaning to number.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swiss crossbowman of folklore, and an old verb meaning to number, as a bank teller does.

clue.text: Final result as forty ponies are assembled

definitions.meaning: the sum reached at the end of adding everything up
in British slang a pony is £25, so forty of them added together make a grand, £1000

explanation.surface: The outcome is decided as forty horses are gathered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ponies' looks like horses but is British slang for £25; forty of them make a grand (£1000) in total.
explanation.definitionFit: The overall sum after everything has been added together is the final figure.
